decks.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe — Part 1: From the French Revolution to 1848
goals: Explain how the French Revolution created a sense of collective identity
Describe how Napoleon's Civil Code spread new ideas, and why people turned against French rule
Describe the aims of the liberal middle classes and the conservative order after 1815
Explain the revolutions of 1830–1848 and the role of romanticism, language and folk culture
Answer a source-based question and a 5-mark question the way examiners mark them

slides.heading: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how the idea of the **nation** was born in France in 1789, spread across Europe with Napoleon's armies, and drove the revolutions of **1830 and 1848**.

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 1: the French Revolution in 1789, the Civil Code in 1804, the Vienna settlement in 1815, the July Revolution in 1830 and the revolutions of 1848
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Today we travel to nineteenth-century Europe. At the start of this story, most Europeans were subjects of kings and emperors. By the end of the century, they saw themselves as members of nations: French, German, Italian, Polish. How did that happen? Watch for three forces as we go: new ideas of liberty, new economic interests, and new feelings stirred by culture. Keep this timeline in mind; examiners love chronology.

slides.heading: What is a nation-state?
slides.body_md: A **nation-state** is a country whose people, ordinary citizens as well as rulers, feel they **belong together** because of a **shared identity and past**, and which is governed in the name of that nation.

rows: Shared identity, history and often language
France after 1789; Germany and Italy by 1871

visual.alt: Table comparing a dynastic empire, held together by loyalty to a ruling family with the monarch sovereign, such as the Habsburg Empire, with a nation-state, held together by shared identity with the people sovereign, such as France after 1789

slides.narration: Think of a nation as a big family that has never met. People who will never see each other still feel they belong together because they share a history, symbols and often a language. A nation-state is a country built on that feeling. In the seventeen hundreds this was rare. Most of Europe was ruled by royal families whose lands were stitched together by marriage and war.

slides.heading: Europe before nations: the Habsburg patchwork
slides.body_md: In the mid-eighteenth century there were **no nation-states** in Europe. The **Habsburg Empire** ruled Austria-Hungary, a patchwork of peoples held together only by **loyalty to the emperor**.

rows: German-speaking aristocracy; Czech and other speakers
About half Magyar-speaking; the rest a mix of other languages
Many other subject peoples, among them Czechs, Slovaks, Slovenes, Croats and Romanians

visual.alt: Table: the Habsburg Empire included German-speaking Alpine regions and Bohemia, Italian-speaking Lombardy and Venetia, Hungary with about half Magyar speakers, Polish-speaking Galicia, and many other subject peoples such as Czechs, Slovaks, Slovenes, Croats and Romanians

slides.narration: Imagine one empire where a farmer, a soldier and a nobleman could not understand each other's language. That was the Habsburg Empire. The only thread joining them was loyalty to the emperor. The landed aristocracy across the empire even spoke French with each other. A shared national identity simply did not exist. Keep this picture in mind: it explains why the Habsburgs feared nationalism so much.

slides.heading: 1789: from subjects to citizens
slides.body_md: The **French Revolution** transferred **sovereignty from the monarch to the people**. The ideas of **la patrie** (the fatherland) and **le citoyen** (the citizen) told the French that they all belonged to one community of equal citizens governed by a constitution.
bullets: Before 1789: the king was the state; people were subjects.
After 1789: the people formed the nation and shaped its destiny.
slides.narration: This is the turning point. Before 1789 the French king said, in effect, I am the state. The Revolution flipped that around: the people are the nation. Two words carried the new idea. La patrie means the fatherland, the shared home of all. Le citoyen means the citizen, a person with rights, not a subject who only obeys. This is the first clear expression of modern nationalism.

slides.heading: How the revolutionaries built a French identity

nodes.label: Ideas: la patrie and le citoyen
Symbols: tricolour flag, new hymns, oaths, martyrs remembered
One market: internal customs duties abolished; uniform weights and measures
One language: French of Paris; regional dialects discouraged

visual.alt: Flow diagram: five kinds of measures, ideas, symbols, an elected assembly, a single market and a common language, all lead to a collective French identity

slides.narration: Here are the five tools the revolutionaries used. New ideas, new symbols like the tricolour and new hymns, an elected National Assembly instead of the old Estates General, one market with uniform weights and measures and no internal customs, and one common language. A neat way to remember them is ideas, symbols, institutions, market and language. In a five-mark answer, one point from each box gives you full coverage.

slides.heading: Exporting the revolution
slides.body_md: The revolutionaries saw it as France's task to **free other European peoples** from autocratic rule.
bullets: Students and educated middle classes set up **Jacobin clubs** in other countries.
French armies carried the idea of nationalism into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy in the 1790s.
slides.narration: The French did not keep these ideas at home. When news of the Revolution spread, students and educated middle-class people in other countries formed Jacobin clubs, named after a political club in Paris. Then came the French armies. As they marched into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and Italy, they carried the idea of the nation with them. Ideas often travel faster than armies, but here they travelled together.

slides.heading: Napoleon's Civil Code: gains and burdens
columns:
**Gains (why some welcomed it)**

- Equality before the law; privileges by birth abolished
- Right to property secured
- Feudal system ended; peasants freed from serfdom and manorial dues
- Guild restrictions removed; transport and communication improved
- Uniform laws, standard weights and measures, a common national currency

**Burdens (why many turned against it)**

- Higher taxes
- Censorship
- Forced conscription: young men made to fight in Napoleon's wars
- Napoleon destroyed democracy in France itself and ruled as emperor

rows: Code exported to Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany

visual.alt: Table: Napoleon took power in 1799, issued the Civil Code in 1804 and then extended it to the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany

slides.narration: Napoleon is a puzzle for many students. He ended democracy in France and made himself emperor, yet he spread revolutionary principles across Europe. His Civil Code of 1804 gave equality before the law and protected property. Businessmen loved the uniform laws and single currency. But the same rule brought higher taxes, censorship and forced conscription. So the welcome turned to hostility. Always present both sides when asked about Napoleon.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Code of 1804
slides.body_md: Which measure of 1804 abolished privileges based on birth?
slides.narration: Try this one before moving on. Think about the year: what did Napoleon issue in 1804?

slides.heading: The liberal middle classes
slides.body_md: **Liberalism** (from the Latin *liber*, free) was the creed of the new **commercial and professional middle classes**.

rows: Individual freedom, equality before the law, government by consent, a constitution, end of autocracy and clerical privilege
Usually only for property-owning men; women and men without property excluded
Freedom of markets; no state restrictions on the movement of goods and capital

visual.alt: Table: political liberalism meant freedom, equality before the law and a constitution; it protected private property; the vote was usually only for property-owning men; economically it meant free markets

slides.narration: Who were the liberals? Mostly the new middle classes: merchants, lawyers, teachers, doctors. They wanted freedom and equality before the law. But notice a contradiction examiners like to test. Equality did not mean the vote for everyone. Most liberals of this time gave the vote only to men who owned property. Women and poorer men were left out. Liberty for some, not yet for all.

slides.heading: Economic liberalism and the Zollverein
slides.body_md: The German lands were divided into **39 states**, each with its own currency, weights and measures. Trade was slow and costly.

nodes.label: Problem: 39 states, many currencies, customs posts at every border
1834: Zollverein customs union, led by Prussia
Tariff barriers abolished; currencies cut from over thirty to two

visual.alt: Flow: the problem of 39 states with many currencies and customs posts leads to the Zollverein of 1834 led by Prussia, which abolished tariff barriers and cut currencies from over thirty to two; railways then linked markets and economic unity strengthened national feeling

slides.narration: Picture a trader carrying cloth across the German lands, stopping at border after border to pay duty and change money. Merchants hated it. In 1834 Prussia led the formation of the Zollverein, a customs union. Tariff barriers fell and the number of currencies dropped from over thirty to two. A railway network soon followed. Economic unity came first, and it made political unity feel natural.

slides.heading: 1815: the conservative order
slides.body_md: After Napoleon's defeat, **Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria** met at the **Congress of Vienna**, hosted by the Austrian Chancellor **Duke Metternich**, to **undo the changes** of the Napoleonic era.

headers: Decision of the Treaty of Vienna (1815)
rows: France lost the territories it had annexed under Napoleon
Kingdom of the Netherlands (with Belgium) in the north; Genoa added to Piedmont in the south
Prussia gained new territories on its western frontier; Austria got control of northern Italy
Russia got part of Poland; Prussia part of Saxony
German confederation of 39 states left untouched

visual.alt: Table of the decisions of the Treaty of Vienna: Bourbons restored, France stripped of annexed lands, buffer states around France, new lands for Prussia and Austria, parts of Poland to Russia and Saxony to Prussia, and the German confederation of 39 states left as it was

slides.narration: The winners of 1815 were conservatives. They believed in tradition: monarchy, the Church, social hierarchy and property. At Vienna they tried to turn the clock back. They restored the Bourbon kings, surrounded France with buffer states and shared out territory among themselves. Note one trap: the German confederation of 39 states was not dissolved. It was left untouched, which kept Germany divided.

slides.heading: Quick check: Vienna, 1815
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Read each statement on its own first. Is the assertion true? Is the reason true? Only then ask whether one explains the other.

slides.heading: Revolutionaries and secret societies
slides.body_md: Conservative regimes were **autocratic**: they **censored** the press, books and the stage to block talk of liberty, and punished dissent. Liberal-nationalists went underground into **secret societies**.
bullets: **Giuseppe Mazzini**, born in Genoa in 1807, joined the Carbonari.
Exiled in 1831, he founded **Young Italy** in Marseilles and then **Young Europe** in Berne.
He believed every people was meant to form its own nation, so Italy must become one unified republic.
Conservatives such as Metternich saw him as a grave threat to the established order.
slides.narration: When open politics is banned, it goes underground. Young men and women formed secret societies to train revolutionaries and spread ideas. The most famous was Giuseppe Mazzini. Exiled at twenty-four, he founded Young Italy and Young Europe. For Mazzini, Italy could not remain a patchwork of small states: it had to become a single republic. Conservatives feared him far more than any army.

slides.heading: Revolutions and risings, 1821–1848

rows: War of independence against the Ottoman Empire; Treaty of Constantinople (1832) recognises Greece as independent
Bourbon king overthrown; constitutional monarchy under Louis Philippe
Uprising in Brussels; Belgium breaks away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands
Armed rebellion against Russian rule crushed
Louis Philippe flees; Republic proclaimed; vote for all men over 21
Liberal revolutions; Frankfurt Parliament meets in May

visual.alt: Table of revolutions from 1821 to 1848: Greek war of independence recognised in 1832, July Revolution in France in 1830, Belgian break-away in 1830, Polish rebellion in 1831, February Revolution in Paris in 1848, and liberal revolutions across German states, Italy and the Habsburg lands in 1848

slides.narration: Between 1830 and 1848 revolution was in the air. Notice how events in France echoed elsewhere: the July Revolution of 1830 was followed by an uprising in Brussels that created Belgium. The Greek struggle drew sympathy from all over Europe, and the poet Lord Byron even went to join it. Learn this table as a chain: when France stirs, its neighbours feel it.

slides.heading: Romanticism: the nation in songs, stories and speech
slides.body_md: **Romanticism** valued emotion and a shared heritage. It found the nation's soul in the culture of **common people**.

rows: True German culture lies with the common people, *das volk*: folk songs, poetry, dances
Collected folk tales; saw French domination as a threat to German culture
Turned folk dances such as the polonaise and mazurka into national symbols in operas and music
Kept using Polish in church when Russian was imposed; many jailed or sent to Siberia

visual.alt: Table: Herder located German culture among common people; the Grimm brothers collected folk tales; Kurpinski made Polish folk dances national symbols; Polish clergy used their language as resistance

slides.narration: Nations are not built only by laws and armies. Romantic writers and musicians said that a nation's true spirit lives in its folk songs, stories and language. In Poland, which had no independent state after being divided between Russia, Prussia and Austria, music and language kept the nation alive. When Russia forced its language on Polish schools, priests kept preaching in Polish. Language became a tool of resistance.

slides.heading: Quick check: language as resistance
slides.body_md: Why did Polish priests keep using Polish under Russian rule?
slides.narration: Think about what a language means to a people who have lost their state. Then choose.

slides.heading: Empty stomachs: economic hardship and revolt
slides.body_md: The 1830s were years of great economic hardship. In 1848, food shortages and unemployment brought the people of Paris onto the streets.

nodes.label: Cheap machine-made goods from England hurt small producers

visual.alt: Flow: population growth leads to migration and slums; cheap English machine-made goods hurt small producers; bad harvests raise food prices; these lead to revolts by Silesian weavers in the mid-1840s and in Paris in February 1848

slides.narration: Ideas alone do not fill the streets; empty stomachs do. Europe's population was rising, but jobs were not. Small producers could not compete with cheap machine-made cloth from England. When harvests failed, bread prices shot up. In Silesia, weavers revolted against contractors who cut their payments. In Paris in 1848, hungry, jobless crowds built barricades, and King Louis Philippe fled. Remember this chain for cause-and-effect questions.

slides.heading: 1848: the liberals' bid for a nation
slides.body_md: Middle-class liberals demanded **a nation-state on parliamentary principles**: a constitution, freedom of the press and freedom of association.

nodes.label: May 1848: elected representatives meet at the Frankfurt Parliament, Church of St Paul
Constitution drafted: a German nation with a monarch whose powers parliament would limit
Crown offered to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia, who rejects it
Aristocracy and army oppose; workers and artisans withdraw support
Troops force the assembly to disband

visual.alt: Flow of the Frankfurt Parliament: meets in May 1848 in the Church of St Paul, drafts a constitution for a German monarchy limited by parliament, offers the crown to the King of Prussia who rejects it, faces opposition from aristocracy and army and loses popular support, and is disbanded by troops

slides.narration: In the German states, 1848 was the liberals' great chance. Elected representatives met in Frankfurt and wrote a constitution. They offered the crown to the King of Prussia, but he refused it from an elected assembly and turned against them. The parliament was dominated by the middle classes and ignored workers' demands, so it lost popular support. Women could only watch from the gallery. Troops ended it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a source-based question, step by step
slides.body_md: Source (written by SOYL): *A Parisian seamstress's imagined diary, February 1848, describes doubled bread prices, closed workshops, barricades, the king's flight, a Republic with votes for men over 21 and national workshops, and a clerk who laughs when she asks about her own vote.*
bullets: Step 1 — Read the questions first, then the source, so you know what to look for.
Step 2 — (a) "Name the king who fled" (1 mark): one precise answer, Louis Philippe. No explanation needed.
Step 3 — (b) "State one promise of the Republic" (1 mark): lift it from the source: votes for men over 21, or work in national workshops.

Step 4 — (c) "What does the clerk's laughter show?" (2 marks): one point from the source (women had no vote) plus one point from your knowledge (women only watched the Frankfurt Parliament from the gallery).
Step 5 — Keep (c) to about 40 words: two clear points, two marks.

rows: Any one promise found in the source
1 for the inference from the source + 1 for linking to wider knowledge

visual.alt: Table: part a is one mark for the correct name; part b is one mark for any promise from the source; part c is two marks, one for an inference from the source and one for a link to wider knowledge

slides.narration: Source questions reward method. Read the questions first so you read the source with a purpose. One-mark parts want one precise fact, often right there in the source. The two-mark part is where marks are lost: examiners want one point drawn from the source and one point from your own knowledge. Notice how the final part asks you to infer: the laughter tells us women had no vote.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 5-mark answer that scores full marks
slides.body_md: Question: *"The first clear expression of nationalism came with the French Revolution." Explain with five points.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Open with one line that answers the question: sovereignty passed from the king to the people.
Step 2 — Plan five different points, one from each box of the identity diagram: ideas, symbols, institutions, market, language.
Step 3 — Write each point as a numbered line with a key term in it (la patrie, tricolour, National Assembly, uniform weights and measures, French as common language).
Step 4 — Do not write five versions of the same point: "flag" and "symbols" together earn only one mark.
Step 5 — Stop at about 120 words; marks come from distinct points, not length.

headers: Key term the examiner looks for
rows: Uniform laws; no internal customs; uniform weights and measures
French as common language; mission to liberate Europe

visual.alt: Table of five points for the model answer with the key term for each, one mark each: la patrie and le citoyen; flag and National Assembly; hymns and oaths; uniform laws and measures; common language and the mission to liberate Europe

slides.narration: A five-mark answer is five separate ideas, each worth one mark. Plan before you write: use the five boxes from our identity diagram. Each point should carry a key term the examiner is scanning for. The most common mistake is repeating one idea in different words, for example writing about the flag and then about symbols. That earns one mark, not two. Short, distinct, numbered points win.

slides.heading: Quick check: Frankfurt, 1848
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Picture the procession of elected representatives walking into a church in Frankfurt. Was it so?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Citizens share an identity; the people are sovereign
la patrie, le citoyen, tricolour, National Assembly, uniform laws, one language
Equality before law, property, end of feudalism; but taxes, censorship, conscription
Freedom, equality before law, constitution, free markets; vote for property-owning men
Vienna settlement hosted by Metternich; undo Napoleonic changes
July Revolution, Belgium, Greece (1832), romanticism, hunger, Paris 1848, Frankfurt Parliament

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: nation-state, French Revolution, Napoleon, liberalism, conservatism and the revolutions of 1830 to 1848 with their key points

slides.narration: Let us pull Part 1 together. The French Revolution made the people the nation. Napoleon spread its reforms but also its burdens. Liberals wanted freedom, a constitution and free markets, while conservatives at Vienna tried to restore the old order. Between 1830 and 1848, revolutions, romantic culture and economic hardship kept nationalism alive, even though the liberals of 1848 failed. In Part 2, we see who finally succeeded.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Dates that are tested: 1789, 1804, 1815, 1830, 1832, 1834, 1848. Practise chronology questions.
Napoleon: always give both sides, reforms and burdens.
Liberal suffrage was for **property-owning men**; do not write "everyone could vote".
Vienna 1815: the German confederation of 39 states was **left untouched**, not dissolved.
Source-based parts: 1-mark answers are precise; 2-mark answers need a source point plus a knowledge point.
5-mark answers: five distinct, numbered points with key terms, about 120 words.
slides.narration: Before your test, check these traps. Many students write that liberals wanted votes for everyone; they did not. Others say the German confederation was broken up in 1815; it was left alone. For source questions, be precise in one-mark parts and combine source and knowledge in two-mark parts. And in long answers, number your points. A tidy answer is easier to mark, and easier to give full marks to.

decks.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe — Part 2: New Nations, Symbols and the Road to 1914
goals: Sequence the unification of Germany under Prussia and of Italy, naming the key actors
Explain how the British nation-state was formed differently
Interpret allegories such as Marianne and Germania
Analyse how Balkan nationalism and imperial rivalry led towards the First World War
Practise map reading and a 5-mark analysis answer

slides.heading: New nations, new symbols, new rivalries
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how **Germany and Italy** were unified, how **Britain** became a nation-state, how artists **pictured the nation**, and how nationalism turned towards **war**.

nodes.label: Prussia and Piedmont take the lead

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 2: liberal attempts fail in 1848, Prussia and Piedmont take the lead, the Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed in 1861, the German Empire in 1871, and the First World War begins in 1914
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome back. In Part 1, the liberals of 1848 dreamed of united nations but failed. In Part 2, the dream comes true, but in a different way: through kings, chief ministers and armies. We will also see how Britain became a nation without a sudden revolution, how artists gave nations a face, and how nationalism, once a dream of freedom, helped lead Europe into war.

slides.heading: After 1848: nationalism from above
slides.body_md: After 1848, nationalism moved away from democracy and revolution. **Conservatives** now used national feeling to **strengthen state power** and political domination over Europe.
bullets: Liberal revolutions were crushed, but the old order could not be fully restored.
Serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg lands and Russia.
In 1867 the Habsburg rulers gave more autonomy to the Hungarians.
slides.narration: Here is a twist. The conservatives who crushed the revolutions of 1848 learned a lesson: nationalism was too strong to ignore. So they began to use it. Kings and ministers now led national movements themselves, to make their states stronger. They also made reforms to calm discontent, like ending serfdom. Remember the phrase nationalism from above. It is the key to Germany and Italy.

slides.heading: Germany: Bismarck's three wars
slides.body_md: Prussia took the lead. Its chief minister **Otto von Bismarck** worked with the **Prussian army and bureaucracy**.

rows: Victory; Austria pushed out of German affairs

visual.alt: Table of Bismarck's three wars: against Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870 to 1871, all won by Prussia, ending with the proclamation of the German Empire

slides.narration: Bismarck did not believe speeches and majority votes would unite Germany. He relied on the army. Over seven years, Prussia fought three wars: against Denmark, Austria and France, and won all three. Each victory pulled more German states under Prussian leadership. Learn the order of opponents with a simple trick: D, A, F, Denmark, Austria, France, in alphabetical order, which is also the order in time.

slides.heading: The road to the German Empire
slides.body_md: The new empire set about **modernising its money, banks, laws and courts**, often copying Prussian practice.

nodes.label: January 1871: William I proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles

visual.alt: Flow: Zollverein in 1834, failure of the Frankfurt Parliament in 1848 to 1849, Bismarck as chief minister, three wars from 1864 to 1871, and the proclamation of William I as German Emperor at Versailles in January 1871

slides.narration: Here is the whole German story on one line. The Zollverein unites the market. The liberals of Frankfurt fail. Bismarck takes charge and wins three wars. In January 1871, in the palace of Versailles, outside Paris, the Prussian king William the First is proclaimed German Emperor. Notice the symbolism: the ceremony was held in the palace of the defeated French kings.

slides.heading: A nation shaped by Prussia
slides.body_md: The unified Germany of 1871 was dominated by **Prussian state power**: its king became emperor, and its army and bureaucracy ran the new state.
bullets: Unity came from above, not through an elected parliament.
The middle-class demand for a single market had prepared the ground.
Nationalism was now linked with state power and the army.
slides.narration: So was Germany made by the people or by Prussia? Examiners often ask you to judge. The best answer gives both sides. Prussian power, the army and Bismarck, did the job. But the ground had been prepared by liberal ideas and by the middle classes who wanted one national market. A strong evaluation answer says: Prussian power completed what liberal nationalism had started.

slides.heading: Quick check: Versailles, 1871
slides.body_md: Who was proclaimed German Emperor in January 1871?
slides.narration: Careful: the man who planned unification and the man who was crowned are different people.

slides.heading: Italy divided
slides.body_md: In the mid-nineteenth century Italy was split into **seven states**. The Italian language had many regional and local variations.

visual.alt: Table: northern Italy was ruled by the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre by the Pope, the south by the Bourbon kings of Spain, and only Sardinia-Piedmont by an Italian princely house

slides.narration: Italy had been divided for centuries. Look at the rulers: Austrians in the north, the Pope in the centre, Spanish Bourbons in the south. Only one state, Sardinia-Piedmont, had an Italian ruling family. That single fact explains why Piedmont led the unification, just as Prussia led Germany.

slides.heading: Three makers of Italy
columns:
**Giuseppe Mazzini** — the dreamer. Founded Young Italy; wanted a unitary Italian republic. Revolts of 1831 and 1848 failed.

**Count Camillo de Cavour** — the diplomat. Chief minister of Sardinia-Piedmont; a cautious statesman, no revolutionary and no democrat; spoke French better than Italian.

**Giuseppe Garibaldi** — the fighter. Led armed volunteers into southern Italy in 1860 and won peasant support.

**King Victor Emmanuel II** — ruler of Sardinia-Piedmont; proclaimed king of united Italy in 1861.

visual.alt: Table: Mazzini used ideas and secret societies, Cavour diplomacy and an alliance with France, Garibaldi armed volunteers, and Victor Emmanuel II royal leadership

slides.narration: Italy was made by very different people. Mazzini supplied the dream of a united republic but his revolts failed. Cavour, a cautious statesman, won through diplomacy. Garibaldi, the fighter, marched south with volunteers. And King Victor Emmanuel the Second gave the new kingdom its crown. A useful phrase: the soul, the brain, the sword and the crown of Italian unity.

slides.heading: The road to the Kingdom of Italy

nodes.label: 1859: Sardinia-Piedmont, allied with France, defeats Austria
1860: Garibaldi drives the Bourbons out of the south
1861: Victor Emmanuel II proclaimed king of united Italy

visual.alt: Flow: Mazzini founds Young Italy in 1831; uprisings of 1831 and 1848 fail; in 1859 Sardinia-Piedmont with France defeats Austria; in 1860 Garibaldi drives out the Bourbons from the south; in 1861 Victor Emmanuel II is proclaimed king of united Italy

slides.narration: Now the steps in order. First the dream and the failed revolts. Then, in 1859, Piedmont and France defeat Austria in the north. In 1860 Garibaldi's volunteers sweep through the south. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel the Second becomes king of Italy. Rome joined a few years later. In a chronology question, anchor yourself with 1859, 1860 and 1861: three years, three steps.

slides.heading: Quick check: put Italy in order
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps in the unification of Italy.
slides.narration: Start with the idea, then the war in the north, then the campaign in the south, then the crown.

slides.heading: Britain: a nation-state without a sudden revolution
slides.body_md: In Britain the nation-state was the result of a **slow process spread over centuries**. The **English**, growing in wealth and power, extended their influence over the other nations of the islands.

nodes.label: 1688: English Parliament seizes power from the monarchy
1707: Act of Union joins England and Scotland
1801: Ireland forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom

visual.alt: Flow: in 1688 the English Parliament seizes power from the monarchy; in 1707 the Act of Union joins England and Scotland; in 1798 the United Irishmen revolt fails; in 1801 Ireland is forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom

slides.narration: Germany and Italy were made in about a decade. Britain took centuries. Before the eighteenth century, people in these islands saw themselves as English, Welsh, Scottish or Irish. The English grew richer and stronger, and Parliament took power from the monarchy in 1688. Through Parliament, the English then drew the other nations in, step by step. No single revolution, just steady English dominance.

slides.heading: Scotland, Ireland and British symbols

rows: Act of Union (1707); British Parliament dominated by English members; Highland Scots lost the right to use Gaelic and wear traditional dress; many were expelled from their homes
Deeply divided between Catholics and Protestants; English helped Protestants dominate; Wolfe Tone's United Irishmen revolt (1798) failed; incorporated in 1801
The Union Jack, the national anthem praising the king, and the English language were actively promoted

visual.alt: Table: Scotland joined by the Act of Union in 1707 and its culture suppressed; Ireland divided by religion, revolt of 1798 failed and incorporated in 1801; new British symbols were the Union Jack, the national anthem and the English language

slides.narration: Becoming British came at a cost for the smaller nations. Highland Scots lost the right to use Gaelic and to wear their traditional dress. Ireland, mostly Catholic, was dominated by a Protestant minority backed by England; a revolt led by Wolfe Tone in 1798 failed, and Ireland was forced into the union in 1801. Then came new symbols: the Union Jack, the anthem and the English language.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading a map of Europe
slides.body_md: Task (practice): *On an outline map of Europe, locate and label A. the city where the Congress of 1815 met, and B. the city of the 1848 parliament.*
bullets: Step 1 — Decode each clue: Congress of 1815 → Vienna; parliament of 1848 → Frankfurt.
Step 2 — Find a landmark you already know: Vienna lies on the river **Danube**, in the east of Austria.
Step 3 — Frankfurt lies on the river **Main**, in western Germany, north of the Alps and east of the Rhine.
Step 4 — Mark each place with a clear dot, write the name beside it, and write the letter (A or B).

slides.heading: Visualising the nation: allegory
slides.body_md: Artists represented a nation as if it were a **person**, usually a **female figure**. Such a figure is an **allegory**: a person or a thing that stands for an abstract idea.

slides.narration: How do you draw something you cannot see, like a nation? Nineteenth-century artists solved it with allegory. They painted the nation as a woman. The female figure did not stand for any real woman; she gave the abstract idea of the nation a concrete form. In France she was named Marianne and appeared on coins and stamps, so people met the nation every day.

slides.body_md: In 1848 the artist **Philip Veit** painted Germania; it hung in the Church of St Paul, where the Frankfurt Parliament met.

Ready to fight for the nation

slides.narration: Allegories are a code, and this table is the key. Examiners often describe an image and ask you to decode one symbol. Learn them in pairs: chains, freed; eagle, strength; oak, heroism; sword, ready to fight; olive branch, peace; rising sun, a new era. And remember the colours black, red and gold: the flag of the 1848 liberals, which is also the flag of Germany today.

slides.heading: Nationalism turns narrow
slides.body_md: By the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism had lost the **hopeful, liberal and democratic** spirit of its early years. It became **narrow and aggressive**, serving the limited aims of states, and nationalist groups grew **intolerant** of each other.
bullets: Major powers used the nationalist aspirations of subject peoples to further their own imperialist aims.
Rivalry grew over trade, colonies, and naval and military might.
slides.narration: Here the story darkens. Early nationalism, in 1789 or in Mazzini's time, spoke of freedom and brotherhood. After 1871, it became narrow and aggressive. Nations now measured themselves by colonies, navies and armies. Big powers even used the national hopes of smaller peoples to grab influence for themselves. This combination of nationalism and imperialism is what you must explain in the Balkans.

slides.heading: The Balkans: a region set to explode
slides.body_md: The Balkans included today's Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, North Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro.

nodes.label: Many peoples (many of them Slavs) with romantic nationalism
New Balkan states with overlapping claims, jealous of each other
Big-power rivalry: Russia, Germany, England, Austria-Hungary
Series of wars in the region

visual.alt: Flow: romantic nationalism among Slav peoples and the break-up of the Ottoman Empire create new Balkan states with overlapping claims; these rivalries and big-power rivalry lead to a series of wars and finally to the First World War in 1914

slides.narration: The Balkans became the most explosive region in Europe. Follow the arrows. Many Slav peoples wanted their own states. The Ottoman Empire that ruled them was crumbling. New states quarrelled over the same land. Meanwhile Russia, Germany, England and Austria-Hungary each tried to extend their control there. Local wars kept drawing in the big powers, until in 1914 they led to the First World War.

slides.heading: Nationalism beyond Europe
slides.body_md: Peoples **colonised by European powers** also took up the idea of the nation. Anti-imperial movements everywhere drew on it, though each built its **own kind of nationalism**.
bullets: The idea that societies should be organised into nation-states came to be accepted as natural and universal.
In India, as you will see in the next chapter, a national movement grew against British rule.
slides.narration: One last idea connects this chapter to the next. The colonised peoples of Asia and Africa learned the language of nationhood, sometimes from their rulers' own history, and turned it against imperial rule. Each anti-colonial movement built its own nationalism. That is exactly what happens in India, in the chapter Nationalism in India. So this European story is also the beginning of ours.

slides.body_md: Question: *Analyse how the Balkan problem became a major cause of the First World War.* (about 120 words)

Step 2 — Point 1 (the region): great ethnic variety; peoples many of them Slavs.
Step 3 — Points 2–3 (inside the region): Ottoman decline and romantic nationalism; new states with overlapping claims and fierce jealousy.
Step 4 — Point 4 (outside the region): Russia, Germany, England and Austria-Hungary competing for control.
Step 5 — Point 5 (the link): local wars drew in the big powers; nationalism plus imperialism led to war in 1914.

sections.heading: 1. The French Revolution and the idea of the nation

key_terms.definition_md: A country whose citizens feel they belong together through a shared identity and past, and in which the people are sovereign.
The fatherland / the citizen: the French Revolution's ideas of a single community of equal citizens.
Describes a monarch whose power is not limited by any constitution or parliament.

rows: No internal customs; uniform weights and measures
French of Paris as the common language

visual.alt: Table of the five kinds of measures the French revolutionaries used, with examples: ideas, symbols, institutions, a single market and a common language

sections.heading: 2. Napoleon and the Civil Code
sections.body_md:
Napoleon ended democracy in France but spread revolutionary principles. The **Civil Code of 1804** (Napoleonic Code):
- abolished **privileges based on birth**, established **equality before the law** and secured the **right to property**;
- was exported to the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany.

Other changes: simplified administrative divisions; **feudal system abolished** and peasants freed from serfdom and manorial dues; **guild restrictions** removed in towns; transport and communication improved; uniform laws, standardised weights and measures and a common national currency helped businessmen and small producers.

**Reaction.** At first French armies were welcomed in many places as bringers of freedom. The welcome soon gave way to **resentment** because of **higher taxes, censorship and forced conscription** into the French armies.

key_terms.definition_md: Napoleon's law code: equality before law, right to property, end of privileges by birth.

rows: End of feudal dues and serfdom
End of guild restrictions; better transport

visual.alt: Table comparing the gains of Napoleonic rule, such as equality before law and the end of feudal dues, with its burdens, such as taxes, censorship and conscription

sections.heading: 3. Liberals, conservatives and revolutionaries (1815–1830s)
sections.body_md:
**Liberalism** (Latin *liber*, free) was the creed of the new middle classes: individual freedom, equality before the law, government by consent, a constitution and representative government, and the inviolability of **private property**. In practice the vote was usually limited to **property-owning men**; women and men without property were excluded. **Economic liberalism** meant freedom of markets and no state restrictions on the movement of goods and capital.

The German lands had **39 states** with their own currencies and measures. In **1834** the **Zollverein**, a customs union led by **Prussia**, abolished tariff barriers and reduced currencies from over thirty to two; a railway network followed.

**Conservatism** after 1815 stressed tradition: monarchy, Church, social hierarchy, property and family. At the **Congress of Vienna (1815)**, hosted by Austrian Chancellor **Duke Metternich**, Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria tried to **undo the Napoleonic changes**. The regimes were **autocratic** and used **censorship**.

**Revolutionaries** worked through secret societies. **Giuseppe Mazzini** (born Genoa, 1807) was exiled in 1831 and founded **Young Italy** (Marseilles) and **Young Europe** (Berne).

key_terms.definition_md: Belief in individual freedom, equality before the law, constitution and free markets.
A belief in keeping traditional institutions (monarchy, Church, social hierarchy, property) and changing society only slowly.
German customs union of 1834 formed under Prussian leadership.

headers: Decision of the Treaty of Vienna
rows: Netherlands (with Belgium) to the north; Genoa to Piedmont
Prussia gains western lands; Austria controls northern Italy

visual.alt: Table of the Treaty of Vienna decisions and their effects: Bourbons restored, France weakened, buffer states created, Prussia and Austria strengthened, and the German confederation left divided

sections.heading: 4. Revolutions of 1821–1848, romanticism and economic hardship
sections.body_md:
- **July 1830, France:** the Bourbon king was overthrown; a constitutional monarchy under **Louis Philippe** was set up. An uprising in **Brussels** led Belgium to break away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
- **Greece:** part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century; war of independence from **1821**; support from Greeks in exile and West Europeans who admired ancient Greece; the poet **Lord Byron** raised funds and went to fight, dying of fever in 1824; the **Treaty of Constantinople (1832)** recognised Greece as independent.
- **Romanticism:** emotion, intuition and shared heritage. **Herder** located German culture in the common people (*das volk*). The **Grimm brothers** collected folk tales. In **Poland**, partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria, **Karol Kurpinski** made folk dances (polonaise, mazurka) national symbols, and the clergy kept using **Polish** as a form of resistance after Russian was imposed; a rebellion in 1831 was crushed.
- **Hunger and hardship:** population growth, unemployment, migration to slums, competition from cheap English machine-made goods, feudal dues on peasants and rising food prices. Weavers in **Silesia** revolted against contractors in the mid-1840s.
- **February 1848, Paris:** food shortages and unemployment led to barricades; Louis Philippe fled; a **Republic** gave suffrage to all **adult males above 21**, guaranteed the right to work and set up **national workshops**.
- **1848, the liberals' bid for a nation:** middle classes demanded a nation-state on parliamentary principles. The **Frankfurt Parliament** (Church of St Paul, May 1848) drafted a constitution and offered the crown to **Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia**, who rejected it. Opposed by the aristocracy and military, and having lost the support of workers and artisans, it was disbanded by troops. **Women** could only watch from the public gallery.
- **After 1848:** serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg lands and Russia; the Hungarians gained more autonomy in **1867**.

key_terms.definition_md: Cultural movement that valued emotion, intuition and a shared heritage, and used folk culture to build national feeling.
Herder's term for the common people, bearers of true national culture.

visual.alt: Timeline table: 1821 Greek war begins, 1830 July Revolution and Belgian uprising, 1831 Polish rebellion crushed and Mazzini exiled, 1832 Greek independence, 1834 Zollverein, 1848 Paris revolution and Frankfurt Parliament

sections.heading: 5. The making of Germany and Italy
sections.body_md:
**Germany.** After 1848, Prussia led the movement for national unity. Chief minister **Otto von Bismarck**, with the Prussian **army and bureaucracy**, fought three wars in seven years, against **Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870–71)**. In **January 1871** the Prussian king **William I** was proclaimed **German Emperor at Versailles**. The new empire modernised its money, banks, laws and courts, often on the Prussian pattern.

**Italy.** Italy was divided into **seven states**: the north under the **Austrian Habsburgs**, the centre under the **Pope**, the south under the **Bourbon kings of Spain**; only **Sardinia-Piedmont** had an Italian princely house. Mazzini's Young Italy aimed at a unitary republic, but revolts in **1831 and 1848** failed. Leadership passed to **Sardinia-Piedmont under Victor Emmanuel II**. Chief minister **Cavour**, a cautious statesman rather than a revolutionary, allied with **France** and defeated **Austria in 1859**. In **1860 Garibaldi** led armed volunteers into the **Kingdom of the Two Sicilies** and, with peasant support, drove out the Spanish rulers. In **1861 Victor Emmanuel II** was proclaimed king of united Italy.

key_terms.definition_md: National unity achieved by a state's rulers, army and diplomacy rather than by a popular or parliamentary movement.

visual.alt: Flow: in 1859 Piedmont and France defeat Austria, in 1860 Garibaldi takes the south, and in 1861 Victor Emmanuel II becomes king of Italy

sections.heading: 6. The British nation-state
sections.body_md: In Britain the nation-state was not the result of a sudden upheaval but of a **slow process spread over centuries**. People had seen themselves as English, Welsh, Scottish or Irish. The **English** nation, growing in wealth and power, extended its influence. In **1688** the English Parliament seized power from the monarchy. The **Act of Union (1707)** joined England and Scotland in the **United Kingdom of Great Britain**; Scottish culture was suppressed (Highland Scots lost the use of Gaelic and their traditional dress; many were expelled). **Ireland**, deeply divided between Catholics and Protestants, saw a failed revolt by **Wolfe Tone's United Irishmen (1798)** and was **forcibly incorporated in 1801**. A new British identity was promoted through the **Union Jack**, the national anthem and the **English language**.

key_terms.definition_md: Union of England and Scotland forming the United Kingdom of Great Britain.

visual.alt: Flow: in 1688 Parliament takes power, in 1707 the Act of Union joins Scotland, in 1798 the United Irishmen revolt, in 1801 Ireland is incorporated

sections.heading: 7. Visualising the nation
sections.body_md:
Artists represented nations as **female figures**: an **allegory** (a person or a thing that stands for an abstract idea). The female figure did not stand for any particular woman; it gave the abstract nation a concrete form.
- **Marianne** (France): popular Christian name; red cap, tricolour, cockade; statues in public squares; image on coins and stamps.
- **Germania** (Germany): crown of oak leaves; painted by **Philip Veit** in 1848 and hung in the Church of St Paul where the Frankfurt Parliament met.

key_terms.definition_md: A person or a thing that stands for an abstract idea, such as liberty or the nation.
Female allegory of the French nation.
Female allegory of the German nation.

sections.heading: 8. Nationalism and imperialism
sections.body_md:
By the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism became **narrow and aggressive**, serving the limited aims of states; nationalist groups grew intolerant of each other, and the big powers used subject peoples' nationalism for imperial aims.

The **Balkans** (today's Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, North Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro) were a region of many landscapes and many peoples; many of their peoples were **Slavs**. Much of the region was under the **Ottoman Empire**, which was breaking up. Romantic nationalism led one subject people after another to break away. The new states claimed overlapping territory and were **fiercely jealous** of each other. **Russia, Germany, England and Austria-Hungary** competed over trade, colonies and naval and military might, each trying to extend control over the region. A series of wars followed, ending in the **First World War (1914)**.

Colonised peoples also took up the idea of the nation: **anti-imperial movements** developed their own kinds of nationalism.

key_terms.definition_md: A policy of extending a country's power and control over other territories and peoples.
South-east European region of many Slav peoples, largely under Ottoman rule in the nineteenth century.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that liberals wanted "votes for all": in this period the vote was mostly for **property-owning men**.
- Saying the Vienna settlement **dissolved** the German confederation of 39 states: it left it **untouched**.
- Mixing up **Bismarck** (chief minister) and **William I** (emperor), or **Cavour** (diplomacy) and **Garibaldi** (volunteers).
- Giving only the good side of Napoleon: always add taxes, censorship and conscription.
- Listing Balkan facts without the **link to 1914**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ, assertion-reason and chronology items: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two distinct points (about 40 words); 3 marks: three points (about 60 words).
- 5 marks: five distinct points with key terms (about 120 words); for "evaluate", a clear judgement backed by evidence and a counter-point.
- Source-based (4 marks): 1 + 1 + 2. One-mark parts are precise facts, often found in the source; the 2-mark part combines a source point with your own knowledge.
- Map work: one mark for each place correctly located and labelled. The board's History map items come from "Nationalism in India".

**Reading sources.** The sources in SOYL practice are written by SOYL for practice; your board paper will give a real source. Read the questions first, underline the clue words, and answer only what is asked.

questions.stem_md: Which measure, introduced in 1804, did away with privileges based on birth and established equality before the law in the areas under French control?

options.text_md: The Treaty of Vienna
The Civil Code (Napoleonic Code)
The Act of Union
The Zollverein agreement

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The 1804 Civil Code, usually called the Napoleonic Code, removed privileges of birth, gave equality before the law and secured the right to property.
Step 2: So the answer is (b).
Step 3: The Treaty of Vienna (1815) restored old rulers, the Act of Union (1707) joined England and Scotland, and the Zollverein (1834) was a German customs union.

questions.stem_md: The French revolutionaries took several steps to create a sense of collective identity among the French people. Which of the following was **not** one of them?

options.text_md: Replacing the royal standard with a new tricolour flag
Renaming the Estates General as the National Assembly
Abolishing internal customs duties and dues
Encouraging regional dialects as the language of government

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The revolutionaries adopted the tricolour, created the National Assembly and abolished internal customs duties: all of these drew people together.
Step 2: They did the opposite with language: the French of Paris was made the common language and regional dialects were **discouraged**.
Step 3: So (d) is the measure they did not take.

questions.stem_md: An illustrative letter written by a shopkeeper in a German town under French rule (around 1810) says: "The new courts are fair and the old tolls are gone, but my taxes keep rising, my newspaper is censored and my son has been taken into the French army." The shopkeeper's mixed feelings are best explained by which statement?

options.text_md: The Zollverein had raised customs duties in the German states.
The Treaty of Vienna had brought back the old princes.
Administrative reforms under Napoleon came with higher taxes, censorship and forced conscription, so the early welcome gave way to resentment.
The Napoleonic Code had given the vote to all adult men.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The letter praises reforms (fair courts, removal of tolls) but complains about taxes, censorship and conscription.
Step 2: That is exactly how many people in conquered areas reacted to French rule: the gains in administration were outweighed by the loss of political freedom and by forced service, so (c).
Step 3: (a) is wrong (the Zollverein **removed** tariff barriers, and only from 1834); (b) is too late (1815); (d) is false: the Code did not give universal male suffrage.

questions.stem_md: For the new middle classes of early nineteenth-century Europe, liberalism in politics stood for

options.text_md: individual freedom, equality of all before the law and government by consent
rule by a hereditary monarch supported by the Church
the right to vote for all adult men and women
the abolition of private property

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Liberalism comes from the Latin *liber*, free. Politically it meant freedom for the individual, equality before the law, a constitution and government by consent.
Step 2: So (a).
Step 3: (b) describes the conservative order. (c) is a common mistake: liberals of this period usually gave the vote only to men who owned property. (d) is the opposite of liberal belief: liberals stressed the inviolability of private property.

questions.stem_md: An imagined petition from merchants of Leipzig in the 1830s says: "Let our wagons pass without a toll at every border, and let buyers and sellers, not princes, decide what goods cross our lands." Which idea does the petition express?

options.text_md: Conservatism
Romanticism
Imperialism
Economic liberalism

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The merchants want goods to move freely, without state-imposed tolls or controls.
Step 2: Freedom of markets and the removal of state restrictions on the movement of goods and capital is economic liberalism, so (d).
Step 3: Conservatism defended the old order; romanticism was about culture and emotion; imperialism is about control over other lands.

questions.stem_md: The Zollverein, a customs union joined by most of the German states, was formed in 1834 at the initiative of

options.text_md: Austria
Prussia
France
Britain

questions.solution_md:
